title: The class meeting
hook: Methodists met weekly in small groups to watch over one another in love

segments.voice: Yesterday, queries: questions Friends carry into the silence. Your line was answer to that of god. Who did you speak to that way, and how did it go? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

Once a week, a handful of people crowd into someone's front room. There's a leader, but no sermon. The leader turns to each person in turn and asks, in one form or another, the same question: how is it with your soul? And each one answers. A hard week at work. A temper that got away. A small joy. A prayer that won't come. Then they pray for one another, and go home. This was the Methodist class meeting, the small weekly gathering of John Wesley's early Methodists. A new room opens here, the Methodist way. Today's word: the class meeting.

How are you is easy. Fine, thanks. How is it with your soul is harder, because it doesn't let you hide behind the weather. That question was the class meeting's whole job. Wesley wrote a short set of General Rules for his societies. They describe the people called Methodists as united to pray together, to hear encouragement, and "to watch over one another in love." Each society was split into small groups called classes, and each class had a leader. The Rules give the leader one task above the rest: to see each person in the class once a week, "to inquire how their souls prosper," and then to advise, correct, comfort or encourage, as the person needed. Methodists tell a story about how it began. The classes started as a way to gather small weekly gifts for the society's needs. But a leader who knocks on doors each week starts hearing things: who's ill, who's drinking, who's quarreling at home. The collecting turned into caring. Watching over one another, in this sense, isn't spying. It's what Paul asks of the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." And what Hebrews asks: "let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." Ordinary people, not experts, holding each other to the life they'd chosen. Some Methodist churches have brought the class meeting back in new forms, and other Christians keep small groups of their own, Bible studies and cell groups and prayer partners. The question underneath is the old one, and it still asks for an honest answer.

Here's the practice: ask the class meeting's question, first of yourself. Let your breath settle. How is it with your soul? Not your inbox, not your health, not your plans. Your soul. Let the answer be honest, even if it's tired, or I don't know. Then bring to mind one person you trust enough to ask the same thing, and picture asking them. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
The class meeting. The weekly Methodist small group, where a leader asked how each soul was doing, and the members watched over one another in love.
Your line: watch over one another. Today, ask one person how is your soul, or something close to it, and then really listen. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Early Methodists met weekly in small classes, where a leader asked each member how it was with their soul and they prayed for one another; some Methodist churches keep class meetings or similar small groups today.

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer says 'today' twice; leader's duties now include 'correct' (the Rules say reprove); closing line no longer tells the listener the question is frightening.

General Rules quotations ('to watch over one another in love'; 'to inquire how their souls prosper') are from memory of the standard text; confirm exact wording. The leader's further duties ('advise, reprove, comfort or exhort') are paraphrased.
The origin story (classes began to collect weekly gifts, often told of Bristol and a penny a week) is told as 'Methodists tell a story'; the place and amount are left out under the claims rule.
'How is it with your soul?' is the traditional form of the class question; the Rules' own wording is 'how their souls prosper'. Confirm.
Original: ἀλλήλων as in Galatians 6:2 (Ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε); confirm.
'Some Methodist churches have brought the class meeting back in new forms' is deliberately general (e.g. covenant discipleship groups); confirm.
